Title: Walking the preferred path: exploring spatial-temporal variation in pedestrian route choice through revealed preferences in a developing city
Affiliations: Lee Kuan Yew Centre for Innovative Cities, Singapore University of Technology and Design, 8 Somapah Road, Singapore, 487372, Singapore
Authors with affiliations: Liu X., Lee Kuan Yew Centre for Innovative Cities, Singapore University of Technology and Design, 8 Somapah Road, Singapore, 487372, Singapore; Wong S., Lee Kuan Yew Centre for Innovative Cities, Singapore University of Technology and Design, 8 Somapah Road, Singapore, 487372, Singapore; Li B., Lee Kuan Yew Centre for Innovative Cities, Singapore University of Technology and Design, 8 Somapah Road, Singapore, 487372, Singapore; Chng S., Lee Kuan Yew Centre for Innovative Cities, Singapore University of Technology and Design, 8 Somapah Road, Singapore, 487372, Singapore; Neo H., Lee Kuan Yew Centre for Innovative Cities, Singapore University of Technology and Design, 8 Somapah Road, Singapore, 487372, Singapore
Abstract: Understanding how and why pedestrians choose their walking routes is crucial for designing inclusive, livable, and sustainable urban environments. However, pedestrian route choice decision-making process remains underexplored, particularly in rapidly developing urban contexts that may lack well-developed infrastructure. Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, presents a compelling case where walkability is increasingly relevant but challenged by infrastructural, environmental, and behavioral complexities. This study adopted a revealed preference approach combining GPS data, street view images, and other geospatial datasets, to examine how path efficiency, street vitality, and streetscape quality influence pedestrian route choice. Using a Path Size Logit model, we found that pedestrians prioritize different factors depending on the time of day and across the CBD, recreational, and commercial urban contexts. While path efficiency consistently influences route choice across all contexts, other factors such as vitality and streetscape quality vary in their importance. These variations result in differing levels of perceived accessibility across central, recreational, and commercial urban areas, diverging largely from objective distance-based measures. Our findings highlight that walkability and perceived accessibility are highly context specific. By capturing these variations, our approach offers context-sensitive accessibility measures that better reflect the perceptions and experiences of pedestrians and support more responsive, evidence-based urban planning, contributing to SDG 10, which seeks to reduce inequality within and among countries by providing more equitable access to opportunities, and SDG 11, which aims to make cities more inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Title: Spatial Heterogeneity and Pandemic Dynamics: Geospatial Insights from Kolkata During Post-Lockdown COVID-19 Spread and Management
Affiliations: Department of Geography, School of Basic and Applied Sciences, Adamas University, West Bengal, Kolkata, India
Authors with affiliations: De S., Department of Geography, School of Basic and Applied Sciences, Adamas University, West Bengal, Kolkata, India; Rai A., Department of Geography, School of Basic and Applied Sciences, Adamas University, West Bengal, Kolkata, India
Abstract: This study explores the spatial and social dynamics of COVID-19 transmission within the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) area, focusing on the post-lockdown period. Using geographically weighted regression (GWR), the research identifies key hotspots and evaluates the effectiveness of public health interventions, such as containment zones. The study highlights significant spatial variations in the spread of COVID-19, with boroughs showing differing relationships between infection rates and socio-economic factors such as population density, slums, and healthcare access. Perception mapping reveals widespread dissatisfaction with healthcare services, including gaps in critical care and vaccination awareness. From a social physics perspective, the chapter underscores the role of human behavior, mobility patterns, and socio-economic conditions in disease propagation. By integrating spatial analysis with social dynamics, the research offers valuable insights for localized pandemic interventions, contributing to broader discussions on how social structures and interactions shape public health outcomes. The findings emphasize the need for data-driven, localized interventions to address regional disparities and improve pandemic management in densely populated urban areas. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024.

Title: Narrowing the healthcare divide: a multivariate analysis of regional disparities in health infrastructure across the Himalayan states of India

Abstract: The Himalayan region of India, characterized by its rugged terrain and dispersed population, faces unique challenges in delivering equitable and accessible healthcare services. Despite numerous government initiatives, substantial gaps persist in the distribution and quality of health infrastructure across the Himalayan states. This study investigates these disparities using secondary data from various published sources. We employed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to develop a Composite Health Infrastructure Index (CHII), ranking the states based on their health infrastructure for the year 2021–22. The rationale behind the study lies in the urgent need to understand and quantify regional inequalities in health infrastructure, which are often masked by national averages. The findings reveal significant discrepancies, with Jammu and Kashmir exhibiting the most advanced infrastructure, while Sikkim ranks the lowest, its CHII being 20 times lower than that of Jammu and Kashmir. A regional comparison indicates that the northern Himalayan states generally outperform their northeastern counterparts, except Assam. Key factors contributing to these disparities include the number of hospital beds per 1,000 population, health facilities per 100,000 population, health professionals per 100,000 population, and overall health expenditure per capita. From a policy perspective, it is crucial to address the structural and logistical barriers that hinder the development of comprehensive and inclusive health infrastructure in the Himalayan region. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2025.

Title: Geographic inequalities in suicide mortality in Italy: Insights from spatial epidemiology
Affiliations: Department of Neuroscience, University of Turin, Turin, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Bevione F., Department of Neuroscience, University of Turin, Turin, Italy; Preti A., Department of Neuroscience, University of Turin, Turin, Italy
Abstract: Background: Suicide mortality displays consistent geographic variation, shaped by environmental, social, and structural determinants. Italy's diverse landscape and regional disparities offer a unique opportunity to investigate the spatial distribution of suicide risk. Aims: This study examines the geographic patterns of suicide across Italy's 110 provinces and evaluates how altitude and population density contribute to regional disparities in suicide mortality. Methods: Using official mortality data from 2006 to 2010, we calculated mean annual suicide rates per 100,000 inhabitants. Spatial autocorrelation was assessed using Moran's I and Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA). Spatial regression models—including the Spatial Autoregressive Model with Spatially Correlated Errors (SAR-SEM)—were applied to account for spatial clustering and examine geospatial predictors. A sensitivity analysis included demographic composition (age and gender) at the provincial level. Results: The national average suicide rate was 5.82 per 100,000 inhabitants, with significant spatial clustering (Moran's I = 0.23, p < 0.0001). High-rate clusters were concentrated in Northern Italy and Sardinia, while low-rate clusters predominated in Southern regions. Altitude and population density were significant predictors, but spatial modeling—especially the SAR-SEM—also identified unmeasured regional factors contributing to suicide patterns. Demographic composition showed weaker and less consistent associations than geographic and spatial factors. Conclusions: Geographic disparities in suicide rates in Italy are linked to altitude and population density, with additional spatially structured influences. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that demographic factors play a limited explanatory role. These findings underscore the value of spatial epidemiology in suicide research and support geographically targeted prevention strategies. © 2025

Title: Spatial and racial covid-19 disparities in U.S. nursing homes
Affiliations: Department of Geography, Florida State University, Bellamy Building, Room 323, 113 Collegiate Loop, PO Box 3062190, Tallahassee, 32306, FL, United States
Authors with affiliations: Wong S., Department of Geography, Florida State University, Bellamy Building, Room 323, 113 Collegiate Loop, PO Box 3062190, Tallahassee, 32306, FL, United States; Ponder C.S., Department of Geography, Florida State University, Bellamy Building, Room 323, 113 Collegiate Loop, PO Box 3062190, Tallahassee, 32306, FL, United States; Melix B., Department of Geography, Florida State University, Bellamy Building, Room 323, 113 Collegiate Loop, PO Box 3062190, Tallahassee, 32306, FL, United States
Abstract: In many parts of the world nursing home residents have experienced a disproportionate risk of exposure to COVID-19 and have died at much higher rates than other groups. There is a critical need to identify the factors driving COVID-19 risk in nursing homes to better understand and address the conditions contributing to their vulnerability during public health crises. This study investigates the characteristics associated with COVID-19 cases and deaths among residents in U.S. nursing homes from 2020 to 2021, with a focus on geospatial and racial inequalities. Using data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and LTCFocus, this paper uses zero-inflated negative binomial regression models, Kruskal-Wallis tests, and Local Moran's I to generate statistical and geospatial results. Our analysis reveals that majority Hispanic facilities have alarmingly high COVID-19 cases and deaths, suggesting that these facilities have the greatest need for policy improvements in staffing and financing to reduce racial inequalities in nursing home care. At the same time we also detect COVID-19 hot spots in rural areas with predominately White residents, indicating a need to rethink public messaging strategies in these areas. The top states with COVID-19 hot spots are Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Illinois, and Oklahoma. This research provides new insights into the socio-spatial contexts and inequities that contribute to the vulnerability of nursing home residents during a pandemic. © 2023 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Access to head and neck cancer specialists: a geospatial analysis of U.S. travel time
Affiliations: Health Data Science, Guidehouse Inc., Tysons, VA, United States; Center for Head & Neck Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, United States; Outcomes Research, Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, United States
Authors with affiliations: Goodnight B.L., Health Data Science, Guidehouse Inc., Tysons, VA, United States; Hanna G.J., Center for Head & Neck Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, United States; Zheng D., Outcomes Research, Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, United States; Habila M., Outcomes Research, Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, United States; Cassese M., Health Data Science, Guidehouse Inc., Tysons, VA, United States; Fortman A., Health Data Science, Guidehouse Inc., Tysons, VA, United States; Walbert H., Health Data Science, Guidehouse Inc., Tysons, VA, United States; Sieling F., Health Data Science, Guidehouse Inc., Tysons, VA, United States; Black C.M., Outcomes Research, Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, United States
Abstract: Introduction: Head and neck (H&N) cancers, a diverse group of epithelial malignancies, significantly impact patients' quality of life and require complex, multidisciplinary care. Despite the need for specialized care, access to H&N cancer specialists is uneven across the United States, leading to disparities in patient outcomes and health equity. To assess geographic disparities in access to H&N cancer specialists in the U.S. and to identify factors contributing to these disparities, with the goal of informing targeted interventions and policies that promote equitable healthcare access. Methods: This geospatial analysis utilized data from various public databases, including the National Provider Identifier Registry, American Society of Clinical Oncology, and U.S. News and World Report, to examine the distribution of H&N cancer specialists relative to incident cancer cases. The study analyzed county-level data across the United States, incorporating demographic factors such as race/ethnicity, age, education, and socioeconomic status. Travel time to the nearest H&N specialist was estimated using the Travel Time API. The analysis included 1,112 H&N specialists (453 surgical oncologists, 346 medical oncologists, and 308 radiation oncologists) identified through self-reported data and relevant fellowships. The primary outcome was the estimated travel time to the nearest H&N specialist, with secondary measures including a disparity index that combined cancer incidence, social vulnerability, and travel time to highlight regions with the greatest access disparities. Results: Significant regional disparities in access to H&N specialists were identified, with non-metropolitan areas and regions outside the Northeast showing notably longer travel times. Socioeconomic and demographics factors, including lower household income, lower insurance coverage, and higher median age, were associated with increased travel times. Disparity Index scores highlighted counties in the South and Western regions as having the highest access disparities. Conclusion: Geographic and socioeconomic disparities in access to H&N cancer specialists contribute to health inequities in the U.S. The disparity index developed in this study provides a valuable tool for identifying high-need areas and guiding policy interventions. Addressing these disparities through targeted resource allocation, mobile clinics, and provider incentives is essential for improving access to specialized care and promoting health equity. Title: Analyzing Inter-District Variations and Determinants of Maternal Health in Jammu Division: a Geospatial Approach
Affiliations: Department of Geography, University of Jammu, Jammu and Kashmir, India
Authors with affiliations: Kumari S., Department of Geography, University of Jammu, Jammu and Kashmir, India; Sharma T., Department of Geography, University of Jammu, Jammu and Kashmir, India
Abstract: This research paper examines the variations in maternal health across different districts of the Jammu Division in the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir.Jammu Division, a geographically and culturally diverse region, presents a unique challenge for maternal health outcomes. The division is marked by a stark contrast in physiography, socio-economic indicators, and cultural practices, which can compound disparities in maternal health across districts. Utilizing secondary data from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) and the Digest of Statistics, Jammu and Kashmir, this study employs a composite index to evaluate the overall maternal health status in each district. Pearson’s correlation method is applied to analyze the relationship between maternal health and various demographic and socio-economic indicators. Geospatial analysis, facilitated by ARC GIS, is used to visualize these disparities and their contributing factors. The findings reveal significant inter-district variations in maternal health outcomes. Districts situated in plain areas, such as Jammu, Samba, and Kathua, exhibit better maternal health performance. This better performance is attributed to higher levels of urbanization, female literacy, less below poverty line (BPL) population, and better infrastructure. In contrast, districts in mountainous regions such as Reasi, Ramban, Doda, and Kishtwar with lower levels of urbanization and higher tribal populations show poorer maternal health indicators. This study provides valuable insights for policymakers aiming to improve maternal health outcomes and reduce regional inequalities within the Jammu Division.Addressing these disparities is crucial for regional planning, asmaternal health directly impacts the socio-economic development and well-being of communities in Jammu Division. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

Abstract: Introduction: Existing evidence suggests a lower uptake of cervical cancer screening among Indian women. Coverage is lower in rural than urban women, but such disparities are less explored. So, the present study was conducted to explore the self-reported coverage of cervical cancer screening in urban and rural areas stratified by socio-demographic characteristics, determine the spatial patterns and identify any regional variations, ascertain the factors contributing to urban-rural disparities and those influencing the likelihood of screening among women aged 30–49 years factors residing in urban, rural, and overall Indian settings. Methods: We did a secondary analysis of the fifth round of the National Family Health Survey in India (2019-21) data with a sample size of 3,48,882 women. The coverage of cervical cancer screening was estimated using sampling weights. Urban-rural differences were compared using the chi-square test. Spatial patterns were analysed using aggregated district-level data, and the contribution of different independent variables to the urban-rural disparities was estimated using multivariate decomposition analysis. Multivariable logistic regression was conducted using STATA 17 to obtain the significant factors of reported screening in urban and rural areas. Results: The nationwide coverage of cervical cancer screening was 2.0% (95% CI: 1.9-2.0). The urban (2.4%; 2.3–2.5) participants had higher screening coverage than their rural (1.8%; 1.7–1.8) counterparts. Moran’s I statistic confirmed the presence of spatial dependence and geographical gradient. Decomposition analysis depicted small urban-rural differences in the screening coverage of 0.60% (0.4–0.8). Endowment and coefficient contributed to 88.15% and 11.85% of the disparities. Compositional changes were contributed majorly by regional differences, low education, scheduled tribes, and having living children > 2. Higher odds of having screening were associated with older age (AOR 1.45, 95% CI: 1.03–1.28), higher education (1.32; 1.13–1.55), higher age of first intercourse (1.60; 1.43–1.79), married (1.25; 1.08–1.45) and diabetic (1.39; 1.17–1.65) women, and those from South India (6.76; 5.90–7.75). The odds were lower among Muslims, scheduled tribes and participants using hormonal contraceptives. Conclusion: There are significant urban-rural disparities in cervical cancer screening uptake that can be attributed to regional variation, educational inequalities, tribal groups, socio-economic inequalities and parity, necessitating the need to comprehensively design tailor-made advocacy initiatives and simultaneously address the broader determinants of health. © The Author(s) 2025.
